I am sympathetic towards his idea of 'multipolarity' vs. 'unipolarity' because I think that the unipolar pretensions of today's USA-dominated Western civilization is why we see third world mass migrations towards our country. Unipolarity provides a rationale to both these immigrants and their fellow travelers (pro-immigrationists): "everyone world citizen has the right to live wherever he wants; the world belongs to us all."

I think Dugin's philosophy provides a valuable conceptual framework to reject this unipolarity.

At the same time, Dugin equates liberalism with the entire Atlanticist block, which he as a Russian nationalists sees as an obstacle to the restauration of Russia's greatness. He argues atlanticism should be undermined. I do not agree; as a Dutch person I think that Europe should either be somewhat of a peacemaker between the Anglosphere and the Russian world, or, if that is not possible, should be part of the Anglo-dominated Atlanticists block.

Unipolarity speaks less to ideological arrangements than security. If the US has very superior military strength the chances of major war are diminished. Europe could plausibly challenge this but only by empowering the EU with an army independent of NATO. Ironically this is something few anti-American European nationalists are prepared to do. And they'd have a hard sell trying to make the case that things would be better as a result. They might get it though if the US implodes.

It is probably a rather moot point though. US power is in relative decline regardless. But with that we're having more and more dangerous clashes with Russia. When NATO bombed Serbia in the 90s Russia was flat on its face and thus no threat militarily. Things have changed. I don't really see that as desirable.

Ideologically though Russia has probably had a mix of influences on the West in recent years. Some have no doubt been good. In some sense our worst enemies are from within and certainly things in addition to Russia.
